title_guess: Raising money for a company: debentures (secured/unsecured, convertible types) vs shares, primary market transactions, and the funding stages angel investor, venture capital, rights issue, private placement and public issue
recurring_cast: instrument_sidebar: cream breadcrumb tree on the left (Capital market -> Securities market -> Corporate security market -> Primary | Secondary market), the current level framed
founder: a blue person with a 'Start' line to a factory labelled NEW PROJECT
sign_badge: a round orange 'NEED MONEY' sticker tilted over the founder all video
RAISE FUNDS bracket splitting into DEBENTURE / BONDS / SHARES, later into Borrow / Make someone Partner
bond_certificate icon for a debenture, share_certificate icon (pie on a certificate) for shares
rupee_note travelling on dotted loops (capital in) with a share_certificate travelling back (equity out)
the funding ladder: founder -> five dark token_squares on arrows (Angel Investor, VC Funding, Rights Issue, Private Placement, Public Issue) -> stock_exchange_building
founder's equity number under the founder (100% struck to 80%, then 60%, 50%, 40%) and each stage's stake in red under its square
ownership_zone: a pink box labelled SHAREHOLDERS that widens to swallow each stage once it has taken equity
question boxes with a big ? (green for 'can assets be sold?', purple for 'can it become shares?')
running_examples: spoken only: borrow 4 lakh rupees by issuing debentures to one lender for 365 days or more
founder's equity ladder on screen: 100% -> 80% (angel 20%) -> 60% (VC 20%) -> 50% (rights issue 10%) -> 40% (private placement 10%)

spoken numbers: 20% to the angel leaves 80%; 20% to the VC leaves 60%; 10% in the rights issue leaves 50%, '50-50 with the shareholders'; the private placement 10% and the 40% are shown but not spoken
spoken only: a rights issue offered at an '80 crore valuation' (the starting valuation falls in a transcript gap); on screen the rights issue is defined as shares at a discounted price

best_moments.why: the instrument names are translated into actions on the tree: DEBENTURE becomes 'Borrow' and SHARES becomes 'Make someone Partner', before any detail
debenture as a two-way exchange: a red elbow carries the debenture from the founder down to a lender while a rupee note slides from the lender to the 'Borrow' branch

primary market transaction: a dotted arrow carries a note up from a blue INSTRUMENT PURCHASER bar to a CAPITAL RAISER bar while a share certificate travels down, so the definition is the picture of two counter-flows
the funding ladder: the founder walks right along five squares to a stock exchange tower; one picture that orders angel, VC, rights issue, private placement and public issue
a grey SKIP band drops over the middle steps with a dotted arc from the founder straight to the public issue: 'these steps are optional' shown, not only said
angel round as a loop: seed capital flows from the angel to the factory on a dotted path, a share certificate marked 20% EQUITY flows back, and the founder's 100% is struck and rewritten 80%
a pink SHAREHOLDERS zone wraps the angel and VC squares, then widens over the rights issue and later the private placement: ownership spreading is a growing box beside a shrinking founder number
the same capital-in / equity-out loop repeats for every round with a new percentage, so the learner reads each new stage by a known pattern

weak_moments.why: the secured/unsecured split appears inside a 9 s transcript gap; the 'can the lender sell the assets?' question is a dense green paragraph box

doubtful fact to verify: the narrator says a fully convertible debenture gives the holder an option and is therefore called OFCD, and the OFCD tag is put on 'Convertible'; usually fully convertible debentures convert compulsorily and only optionally convertible ones give the choice. 'Semi-convertible' is more often called partly convertible
seed capital's purpose, the minimum viable product, is spoken but not drawn
'High net worth individuals' is written among the angel traits but not spoken there; angel traits are a fan of five text lines
the VC firm (rich individuals pool money, a fund manager invests it for profit) is spoken over a still screen with only a 'Venture Capital Firm' tag

doubtful arithmetic to verify: each new investor's stake is taken only from the founder (the angel stays at 20% after the VC round); a new share issue normally dilutes every existing holder in proportion, and in a rights issue the founder, as an existing holder, could keep their share by buying
about 43 s with one change: the cost and time of an IPO (adverts, newspapers, months) vs one or two meetings in a private placement are spoken while only a two-line BENEFITS note sits on screen
about 50 s almost still at the end: 'no fixed order', 'angel and VC only early', 'rights issue and private placement can repeat' and listing after an IPO are spoken; only a small IPO arrow is added
app promotion overlay over the lower left at the close

segments.teaches: the securities market lends and borrows for 365 days or more using shares, bonds and debentures; bonds were done last time; debentures mean borrowing, shares mean taking partners

elements.what: left sidebar: CAPITAL MARKET -> Securities Market -> Corporate Security Market (framed) -> Primary / Secondary Market
blue founder with a 'Start' line to a factory labelled NEW PROJECT on a cream band
round orange NEED MONEY sticker
RAISE FUNDS splitting into DEBENTURE, BONDS, SHARES with certificate icons
green box on BONDS with a hand-written 'Done!' tick, then BONDS removed
grey box on DEBENTURE with 'Borrow' under it

segments.notes: 6 change events in 45 s. The three instruments appear at 2 s, about 15 s before they are spoken. Bonds are ticked 'Done!' and removed: the previous video closed on screen.
segments.idea: a company that needs long-term money can issue debentures, bonds or shares; today: debentures and shares
segments.shown_as: a founder walks a 'Start' line to a factory under a NEED MONEY sticker; RAISE FUNDS branches into three certificates; bonds get a green 'Done!' tick and drop out, and the debenture is greyed with 'Borrow' under it

segments.teaches: a debenture is a loan: the company gives a debenture to a lender, gets cash, and repays the principal with yearly interest as per the debenture's terms

elements.what: RAISE FUNDS now splits into Borrow and Make someone Partner
blue lender figure at the left
red elbow from the founder through a DEBENTURE certificate down to the lender
green rupee note sliding from the lender to 'Borrow'
under the lender: gets the principal back with annual interest as per the debenture's terms

segments.notes: 4 change events in 35 s. The 4 lakh rupee loan is spoken but no number is drawn. 'interest' is bold in the caption.
segments.idea: debenture out, cash in; later principal plus interest go back
segments.shown_as: the tree relabels itself Borrow / Make someone Partner; a red elbow carries a debenture from the founder down to a lender, a rupee note slides from the lender into 'Borrow', and a caption promises principal plus yearly interest
segments.example: spoken only: borrow 4 lakh rupees for 365+ days

segments.teaches: first test of a debenture: if the company cannot repay, can the holder sell its assets? yes = secured, no = unsecured; the unsecured holder takes more risk and so gets higher interest

elements.what: the raise-funds tree fades to grey
two small numbered circles, i and ii, beside the debenture
big ? on a green box joined to circle i
green box: if the issuer cannot repay with interest, can the amount be paid by selling the company's assets?
branches Un-Secured DEBENTURE and Secured DEBENTURE
[HIGH INTEREST] under Un-Secured

segments.notes: 7 change events in 40 s. The branches appear at 98.4 s, inside a transcript gap (97.1-106.0 s), so the naming of secured/unsecured is not heard. Risk-to-interest is a written tag only.
segments.idea: whether assets back the loan decides secured vs unsecured, and less backing means more interest
segments.shown_as: the old tree fades; two numbered circles pop beside the debenture; circle i links to a green question box under a big ?, which splits into unsecured and secured debentures, and HIGH INTEREST writes under the unsecured one

segments.teaches: second test: can the debenture later be turned into shares? gives non-convertible, convertible and semi-convertible debentures; a convertible one with an option is called OFCD

elements.what: big ? on a purple box joined to circle ii
purple box: in future, is there an option to convert this debenture into shares?
branches Non-Convertible, Convertible and Semi-Convertible DEBENTURE
green box on Convertible with an OFCDs tag

segments.notes: 7 change events in 50 s. Same pattern as the first test (numbered circle -> question box -> branches). The narrator says 'fully convertible' while the screen says 'Convertible'; the OFCD explanation should be verified (see weak moments).
segments.idea: whether a debenture can become shares decides its convertible type
segments.shown_as: the green test swaps for a purple question box from circle ii under a big ?, which splits into non-convertible, convertible and semi-convertible debentures; the convertible branch glows green and gets an OFCDs tag

segments.teaches: shares: people who give money become partners and owners in proportion to what they put in; no repayment, but they share profit and loss; a sale of new shares from the capital raiser to the instrument purchaser is a primary market transaction

elements.what: raise-funds tree back with Borrow and Make someone Partner
blue underline under Make someone Partner
four blue partners in a pale-blue box, an arrow dropping to each
these have become owners in proportion to their % contribution
dotted arrow up carrying a rupee note; dotted arrow down carrying a share certificate
blue bars CAPITAL RAISER (top, at the founder) and INSTRUMENT PURCHASER (bottom, at the partners)
sidebar frame moves to Primary Market

segments.notes: 12 change events in 52 s (about every 4 s): the busiest stretch. Recap of debentures first (tree restored), then the partner route. The sidebar move to 'Primary Market' names where the transaction happens.
segments.idea: selling new shares turns lenders into owners; that direct sale is the primary market
segments.shown_as: the tree comes back, 'Make someone Partner' is underlined and four partners drop into a box as owners by contribution; a note climbs a dotted line from them to the founder while a share certificate drops the other way; the two ends are tagged INSTRUMENT PURCHASER and CAPITAL RAISER and the sidebar frame jumps to Primary Market

segments.teaches: ways to raise equity in the primary market: angel investing, VC funding, rights issue, private placement and public issue (IPO, which lists the company; a later public issue is an FPO); the steps are not compulsory and a company can go straight to a public issue

elements.what: founder -> five dark squares on green arrows
stalk labels at staggered depths: Angel Investor, VC Funding, Rights Issue, Private Placement, Public Issue
stock exchange tower labelled STOCK EXCHANGE at the end
grey band lettered SKIP over the middle squares, with a dotted arc from the founder to the public issue

segments.notes: 9 change events in 64 s. Each label lands on its spoken name. IPO and FPO are spoken only (no labels yet). The SKIP band stays about 7 s.
segments.idea: a company climbs through funding stages towards the stock exchange, but may skip straight to a public issue
segments.shown_as: the founder sets off along a row of five squares joined by arrows towards a stock exchange tower; each square's name drops on a stalk as it is spoken; a grey SKIP band covers the middle squares while a dotted arc jumps from the founder to the public issue

segments.teaches: an angel investor puts a small early sum (seed capital, even at the idea stage) into the company in return for equity: 20% to the angel leaves the founder 80%; angels are early, use their own money, may mentor, and can be family or relatives

elements.what: blue factory beside the founder marked 100%, arrow to the Angel Investor square
dotted loop with a rupee note from the angel back to the factory, labelled SEED CAPITAL
red dotted path carrying a share certificate marked 20% EQUITY from the founder to the angel
100% struck, 80% written above
fan of lines from the angel: Early stage investor, High net worth individuals, Invests their own money, May provide mentorship, Sometimes a family member or relative

segments.notes: 9 change events in 89 s. The first full capital-in / equity-out loop; it is reused for every later round. 'Minimum viable product' is spoken but not drawn; 'High net worth individuals' is written but not spoken here.
segments.idea: early money comes in, a slice of ownership goes out, and the founder's share drops
segments.shown_as: the chain zooms to founder, factory and the first square; a rupee note runs a dotted loop from the angel into the factory (SEED CAPITAL) while a share certificate marked 20% runs back on a red dotted line; the founder's 100% is struck to 80% and five traits fan out from the angel

segments.teaches: after a working first product, a bigger sum for production and marketing comes from a venture capital firm (pooled money of rich individuals run by a fund manager) for equity: 20% more leaves the founder 60%; several VC rounds and firms are possible

elements.what: ladder back with 80% under the founder and 20% under Angel Investor
blue 'Venture Capital Firm' tag on the VC square
pink column over VC Funding
dotted CAPITAL loop with a note from the VC to the factory; red dotted EQUITY 20% path back
ladder returns with 60% under the founder and 20% under VC

segments.notes: 8 change events in 70 s. Zoom out to the ladder, zoom in to the next stage, zoom out with the new numbers: a three-beat rhythm that repeats. The VC fund structure is spoken over a still screen.
segments.idea: the second, bigger round comes from a VC firm and takes another slice of ownership
segments.shown_as: the ladder returns with 80% and 20% written in; the view closes on the VC square, which gets a Venture Capital Firm tag and a pink column; capital loops into the factory and a 20% equity certificate goes back; the ladder returns with the founder at 60%

segments.teaches: everyone given equity is a shareholder; a rights issue offers existing shareholders more shares (on screen: at a discounted price); diluting 10% more leaves the founder 50%

elements.what: pink zone round the Angel and VC squares labelled SHAREHOLDERS
lavender box on Rights Issue
definition beside a purple bar: the company offers existing shareholders additional shares at a discounted price
CAPITAL loop from the shareholder zone to the founder, EQUITY 10% back
'existing shareholders' boxed inside the definition
60% struck, 50% written; 10% under Rights Issue

segments.notes: 9 change events in 64 s. The rights issue money is drawn as coming from the existing shareholder zone, which is the point of a rights issue. Part of the spoken example falls in a transcript gap (464.1-473.2 s); the spoken '80 crore valuation' is not drawn, and 'discounted price' is written but not spoken.
segments.idea: a rights issue raises more money from the people who already own the company
segments.shown_as: a pink SHAREHOLDERS zone wraps the angel and VC; the rights-issue square is boxed and its definition writes on with 'existing shareholders' boxed; capital loops from the zone to the founder, 10% equity goes back and the founder's 60% is struck to 50%

segments.teaches: a private placement sells shares directly to a small group of selected outside investors (institutions, rich individuals) at a negotiated price, without going public

elements.what: ladder back with 50% at the founder, 10% under Rights Issue
SHAREHOLDERS zone widens over the rights issue
pale-blue note on a brace beside Private Placement: small number of select investors, typically institutions or rich individuals
capital loop from the private placement to the founder, EQUITY 10% back
50% struck, 40% written

segments.notes: 6 change events in 81 s. The 10% stake and the founder's new 40% are shown but never spoken. A real business group is named in speech as an example investor (not shown).
segments.idea: a big company can sell a slice to a few chosen investors directly
segments.shown_as: the ladder returns at 50%; the shareholder zone grows over the rights issue; a note on the private placement names its few chosen investors; capital loops in, a 10% equity certificate goes out and the founder's 50% is struck to 40%

segments.teaches: private placement is cheaper and quicker than a public offering: no adverts or long process, a deal in one or two meetings, win-win

elements.what: BENEFITS: less costly and less time-consuming than a public offering

segments.notes: 1 change event in 43 s. The IPO's adverts, newspaper notices and long process, and the one-or-two-meeting deal, are spoken only.
segments.idea: a private deal saves the cost and time of a public offer
segments.shown_as: a two-line BENEFITS note writes on above the private-placement note; the rest of the canvas stays still

segments.teaches: private-placement buyers become shareholders too; stages need no fixed order (angel and VC come early, rights issues and private placements can repeat); a public issue starts with an IPO and the company is then listed so shares can be traded

elements.what: full ladder with 40% at the founder and 10% under Private Placement
SHAREHOLDERS zone widens over the private placement
green arrow from Public Issue down to IPO

segments.notes: 2 change events in 63 s, plus a small IPO arrow near the end. 'No fixed order' and 'listing lets shareholders sell and new buyers enter' are spoken over a still ladder.
segments.idea: after the private rounds, a public issue (IPO) opens the company to everyone and lists it
segments.shown_as: the whole ladder returns with the founder at 40%; the pink shareholder zone stretches over the private placement; a small arrow drops from Public Issue to IPO
segments.example: final split shown: founder 40%, angel 20%, VC 20%, rights issue 10%, private placement 10%

segments.teaches: end screen: app promotion, next video and playlist

elements.what: phone mock-up promo over the canvas, then next video and playlist panels
